name: Hayward Regular Black Hole
description: A black hole with two horizons and a regular centre, Schwarzschild's metric far away and de Sitter space at the core. Sean Hayward wrote it down in 2006 and let its mass change in time, so that a region of trapped surfaces forms, evaporates, and leaves neither a singularity nor an event horizon.
convention: The mass is the length $m = GM/c^2$, and the length $\ell$ sets the cosmological constant $3/\ell^2$ of the de Sitter core at the centre. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: What sits at the centre of a black hole? Roger Penrose's theorem of 1965 says that once gravity has trapped light a singularity follows, given a Cauchy surface and matter of positive energy density [penrose1965]. At a conference in Tbilisi in 1968 James Bardeen presented a black hole with horizons, a regular centre, and matter obeying the weak energy condition, the first of its kind [hayward2006, ansoldi2008, borde1997]. Andrei Sakharov had already proposed that matter at very high density has a pressure equal to minus its energy density, and Erast Gliner that a vacuum of that kind could replace the singularity at the end of a collapse [ansoldi2008]. Irina Dymnikova's exact solution of 1992 is Schwarzschild's far away and de Sitter's near the centre, with no singularity anywhere [dymnikova1992].¶Sean Hayward published his own in 2006 and called it a "minimal model" [hayward2006]. He asked two things of $F = g^{rr}$ in a static, spherically symmetric metric: that it go over to Schwarzschild's $1 - 2m/r$ far away and to $1 - r^2/\ell^2$ at the centre [hayward2006]. His choice, "a particularly simple metric satisfying the above conditions", was $$F(r) = 1 - \frac{2mr^2}{r^3 + 2\ell^2m},$$ which is Schwarzschild's at $\ell = 0$ and flat space at $m = 0$ [hayward2006]. Near the centre its Einstein tensor is that of a cosmological constant $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$, so the core is de Sitter space of radius $\ell$ whatever the mass [hayward2006, frolov2016]. Hayward expected $\ell$ "to be the Planck length or of the same order, though larger length scales are not excluded" [hayward2006]. He noted that Eric Poisson and Werner Israel had derived an equivalent $g^{rr}$ in 1988, from a vacuum energy density proportional to the square of the curvature [hayward2006, poisson1988].¶The zeros of $F$ are the horizons, and their number depends on the mass [hayward2006]. Below $m_* = 3\sqrt{3}\,\ell/4$ there are none, at $m_*$ one degenerate horizon sits at $r = \sqrt{3}\,\ell$, and above it there are two, near $2m$ and near $\ell$ once $m \gg m_*$ [hayward2006]. Hayward's comment: "Note the existence of a mass gap: such black holes cannot form with mass $m<m_*$" [hayward2006]. With two horizons the causal structure is Reissner-Nordström's, "with the internal singularities replaced by regular centres" [hayward2006]. Read through the Einstein equations, the metric needs matter that obeys the weak energy condition and whose density falls off as $r^{-6}$ [hayward2006, bambi2013]. That matter breaks the strong energy condition near the centre, and the inner horizon is a Cauchy horizon, so the singularity theorems do not apply [hayward2006, lan2023].¶A static black hole has neither a birth nor a death, so Hayward rewrote the metric in advanced time $v$, $$ds^2 = -F\,dv^2 + 2\,dv\,dr + r^2d\Omega^2,$$ and let the mass depend on it, $m(v)$ [hayward2006]. At $\ell = 0$ and at large radius this is Prahalad Vaidya's radiating metric of 1951, and the one new component of the Einstein tensor is the ingoing flux $G^r{}_v = 2r^4m'/(r^3 + 2\ell^2m)^2$ [hayward2006, vaidya1951]. While the mass grows the radiation carries positive energy, while it falls the energy is negative, and the centre stays regular throughout: "It seems that the effective cosmological constant protects the core" [hayward2006]. The two trapping horizons appear together when the mass passes $m_*$ and vanish together when it falls back, joined into one smooth closed curve around a compact region of trapped surfaces [hayward2006]. For the outgoing Hawking radiation he adapted an idea of William Hiscock, a surface outside the hole where pairs are created, with the same metric in retarded time beyond it, and he thanked Bardeen "for pointing out the surface layer" there [hayward2006, hiscock1981]. Once the mass is gone flat space is left, and "There is no singularity and no event horizon" [hayward2006].¶Hayward never wrote the word information [hayward2006]. "Most discussions of black-hole evaporation mention a certain I-word, as a paradox, problem or puzzle", and his spacetimes, regular and with the causal structure of flat space, "show that this word need not be mentioned" [hayward2006]. He paraphrased an old adage: "what goes in, must come out" [hayward2006]. The closed trapping horizon had been conjectured before, by Valeri Frolov and Grigory Vilkovisky in 1981 and by Thomas Roman and Peter Bergmann in 1983 [hayward2006, frolov1981, roman1983]. In 2014 the same metric occurred to Frolov independently, and Bardeen told him of Hayward's paper [frolov2014]. Frolov showed with it that quanta trapped during the evaporation come back out once it is over, with a very large blueshift [frolov2014].¶Could anything simpler do the job? No $g^{rr}$ that is a ratio of polynomials of degree two or less describes a regular black hole, Frolov proved in 2016, and his family of degree three contains Hayward's [frolov2016]. A clock at Hayward's centre keeps time with a clock at infinity, since $F = 1$ at both [delorenzo2015]. A physical metric should have a time delay there, Tommaso De Lorenzo, Costantino Pacilio, Carlo Rovelli, and Simone Speziale argued in 2015, and they modified Hayward's to carry one [delorenzo2015]. The regular core, Raúl Carballo-Rubio, Francesco Di Filippo, Stefano Liberati, Costantino Pacilio, and Matt Visser argued in 2018, is exponentially unstable to perturbations while the evaporation takes an infinite time [carballorubio2018]. Its shadow has met the Event Horizon Telescope's image of Sagittarius A*, and in the analysis of Sunny Vagnozzi and fourteen coauthors in 2023 every $\ell$ up to the extremal one passed [vagnozzi2023].

related.text: Hayward's black hole at $\ell = 0$, where the core shrinks away and the singularity is back, with $r_s = 2m$ [hayward2006].
The same two horizons and the same tower of regions. Reissner-Nordström's has a timelike singularity at $r = 0$, and Hayward's a regular centre [hayward2006].
The first regular black hole, from 1968, with $(r^2 + g^2)^{3/2}$ where Hayward's has $r^3 + 2m\ell^2$. Hayward called his own "similar to the Bardeen black hole" [hayward2006].

The core. Near the centre $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$, de Sitter's static metric with $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$, and as $m \to \infty$ at fixed $\ell$ the whole metric becomes de Sitter's [hayward2006, frolov2016].
The forming and evaporating hole at $\ell = 0$, and at large radius for every $\ell$. Vaidya's ingoing radiation makes a singularity at the centre [hayward2006].

Another black hole with no singularity. Simpson and Visser set theirs apart from the regular black holes of Bardeen and Hayward: it opens through a throat of radius $a$ where Hayward's closes over a regular centre [simpson2019].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2mr^2/(r^3 + 2m\ell^2)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Length of the de Sitter core, with $F \approx 1 - r^2/\ell^2$ near the centre; $\kappa_\pm$ are the surface gravities of the horizons $r_\pm$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - 2mr^2/(r^3 + 2m\ell^2)\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$. For $\ell < 4m/3\sqrt{3}$ the horizons $r_- < r_+$ are the two positive roots of $r^3 - 2mr^2 + 2m\ell^2$.
